The digits are 1967, confirmed by the English parenthetical. The "a" sitting inside them is a folio marker that has collided with the numeral in the source, not a Tibetan letter. Contiguity forbids trimming it, so the whole damaged token maps to the clean English numeral; a cleanup pass may want to split the apparatus out. ENGLISH LEFT UNWRAPPED, deliberately and correctly: the entire third sentence, "************ The following is a list of the scenes found in the middle of the blockprint chart just described." — that is GMR's editorial bridge into the caption series and has no Tibetan licensor anywhere in this segment. Also unwrapped: the asterisk rule, every article, "was", "has been", both auxiliaries, all four "of", all three "in", and all punctuation. JUDGMENT CALLS A REVIEWER MAY WANT TO OVERTURN. (a) zhus -> "completed": zhus is properly "was requested / edited / executed", and "completed" is GMR's rendering, not the lexical sense; it is also the only verb available in that English sentence. (b) 'di -> "itself": a plain demonstrative rendered as an emphatic. Note that the English "this" in sentence one is NOT the exponent of this 'di — the Tibetan of that clause (par gyi 'du byed) has no demonstrative at all, so that "this" is the translator's addition and linking 'di across to it would be a false cross-clause link. (c) sbas gnas -> "Bene": sbas gnas is "hidden place/land", and sbas gnas 'bras mo ljongs is Sikkim, "the hidden land of Dremo Jong". GMR phoneticizes sbas gnas rather than translating it; by project rule his spelling is preserved exactly and the span links to it as written.

AI NOTE — Caption for scene 1 of the elephant-path chart, the first of the nine mental states (sems gnas dgu). Wylie: `1a/sems 'jog pa`. English: `[1] 1) Setting the mind on the object`. Three syllables of actual text, all covered; one apparatus token. CROSS-REFERENCE — the caption matches the prose exactly. Segment 157 lists the nine states and renders this same compound "setting the mind on the object", word for word; the caption differs only in capitalization and the added numbering. Segment 158 then attaches it to the first of the six powers (thos pa'i stobs, learning the instructions), and segment 159 puts it in the first mode of focus (bsgrims te 'jug pa, forceful concentration). Segment 170's caption ("4a/") repeats that attachment on the chart itself. So "setting the mind on the object" is HGM's fixed rendering for sems 'jog pa across this course, not a caption-only expansion — but see below: fixed rendering is not the same as licensed text. UNWRAPPED, deliberately: - "[1]" and "1)" — editorial numbering supplied in the English edition. The Tibetan carries no numeral (no gcig); "1a/" is the chart's scene key, handled as apparatus at s1 rather than linked to either. - "the" (twice in 37 characters) — article, and unlinkable under the repeated-function-word rule regardless of licensor. - "on the object" — the reading most at risk of over-capture, and both analysts independently refused it. sems 'jog pa is literally "placing/setting the mind"; there is no la/su/tu case particle and no yul or dmigs pa anywhere in these three syllables to license an object phrase. Compare segment 156, where the object of meditation IS present in the Tibetan (dmigs pa'i ka ba) and licenses "the object of your meditation" — that is what a licensor looks like. Here HGM supplies it from the standard gloss of the first state. Correct English; no exponent. Folding it into 'jog pa would be exactly the measured dominant defect. "on" likewise stays loose: no case particle, and it is not part of the English verb "set" as governed here. BOUNDARY: "mind", not "the mind", for sems — the tighter span, and the article is unlinkable anyway. ORDERING/CROSSING: spans run in strict forward wylie order (1a/ → sems → 'jog pa → pa), which inverts the English — "Setting" (s3) precedes "mind" (s2) on the page. Verb-final Tibetan against a verb-initial English gerund; the renderer should expect the eng spans to cross here, as they will in every caption of this series that nominalizes a verb (168 dran pa, and the byed pa / 'jog pa captions further down the chart). RECONCILIATION: the two proposals agreed on every English link and on the d=7 placement of pa; neither over-captured. The only divergence was whether to carry the scene marker as a span. Kept, null-glossed — it makes no English claim, and it labels the token as apparatus instead of leaving an unexplained "1a/" adjacent to text. Depths audited against rule 3: no bound morpheme sits at d=6, and there are no standalone particles in this caption, so there is no d=6 layer at all.

AI NOTE — Two-word caption, three spans, no padding. dran pa is the sole content term (mindfulness/recollection); Geshe Michael renders it by its function rather than lexically, so the linked English is one unitary rendering of one term and is wrapped as a single d=5 span rather than decomposed — no morpheme licenses "back" and nothing sub-lexical would survive checking. BOUNDARY RULING: the span stops at "Bringing the mind back". "to the object" is left UNWRAPPED — there is no dmigs pa, no yul, and no la/tu/du anywhere in the wylie to license it. It is HGM's standing amplification of this term, not a translated element: compare §156, where the verse's "to your object" is licensed by an actual dmigs pa, and §167, where "the mind" is licensed by an actual sems ('sems 'jog pa'). Neither licensor is present here. "the mind" is kept inside s2 only because English requires an object for "bring back"; it swallows no competing Tibetan word. "[2]" stays unwrapped as editorial numbering — per the standing rule numerals belong to gcig/gnyis/gsum, and there is no gnyis here. The nominalizer pa is d=7, not d=6: it is bound inside the d=5 span above it, and listed flat it would match the trailing syllable of the same word and break the forward cursor. Span order follows the wylie: 2a/ (offset 0) → dran pa (offset 3) → the child pa (offset 8 inside its parent). CHART CONTEXT, checked against the source: '2a/' is a SCENE marker, not a folio side. The markers run 1a/ … 9a/ at §167–§175 and then 1a0/, 1a1/, 1a2/ … at §176ff (ACIP-numeral 10, 11, 12), one-for-one with the editor's [1]…[16], and §166 introduces the whole run as "a list of the scenes found in the middle of the blockprint chart". Do not gloss it as folio 2 side a. CROSS-REFERENCE for the translator: this caption does NOT match a prose mental state. The nine states named at §157 carry a second, parenthetical numeral in their captions — §167 is "[1] 1) Setting the mind on the object" and §175 is "[9] 2) Keeping the mind on the object with brief continuity" — and §168 has no such numeral. It belongs instead with the chart's symbolic elements ([3] shes bzhin, [5] the elephant = the mind, [6] the monkey = distraction); §156's root verse identifies dran pa as the rope ("dran pa'i thag pas"). Distinguish it also from §178 'dran pa'i ltobs so' = "[12] The power of bringing the mind back to the object", which is the six-powers caption for the same term (the third power, achieving states three and four, per the prose at §158). §158 and §178 render dran pa with the full "…to the object" tail; the identical tail here is therefore expected HGM idiom and correctly left loose rather than linked. Note in passing that §178's wylie reads 'ltobs' for stobs — a source typo, preserved byte-for-byte by project rule.
C03/c3p57: AI NOTE — Verbatim source — wylie: "3a/shes bzhin"; english: "[3] Watchfulness". Confirmed against the spine. Two spans. The caption's only content word is "Watchfulness", and the only Tibetan licensing it is the compound shes bzhin (Skt. samprajanya), HGM's standard equivalent. The capital W is his, preserved byte-for-byte. Note the wylie has no space after the panel marker ("3a/shes"), so s2 begins exactly at "shes"; both tib strings are contiguous substrings in forward order and survive a forward-only walk. Deliberate non-links: - "[3]" — editorial numbering in the English, matching "3a/" in the wylie. Neither is text. Left unwrapped rather than glued to the noun; numerals belong to gsum, not to shes bzhin. Compare §167, whose English carries BOTH the panel number and a list number ("[1] 1) Setting the mind on the object") — proof that the bracketed figure is apparatus and not part of any caption's wording. - No d=7 split of shes / bzhin. Rejected from proposal A on two counts. Evidentially, neither member has its own exponent inside the single word "Watchfulness", so both children would carry eng null and add nothing. Mechanically, a d=7 "shes" sits at wylie offset 3, behind the cursor at 13 left by "shes bzhin", and the forward-only generator would refuse the page. Per the no-padding rule the caption stops at two spans. For the translator — the cross-reference asked for, and it does NOT go where you would expect. shes bzhin is not one of the nine mental states: §157 lists all nine (sems 'jog pa … mnyam par 'jog pa) and shes bzhin is absent. The stage-name captions are §167 (sems 'jog pa, state 1) and §175 (rgyun du 'jog pa, state 2). Captions §168–169 label the two implements from the Madhyamaka-hrdaya verse quoted at §156 — dran pa'i thag pa, the rope, and the hook — so caption 3 names a faculty, not a stage. Two wording crossings worth flagging: 1. Against the prose, this caption matches. §158 renders shes bzhin gyi stobs as "the power of watchfulness" — same equivalent, same course, so "Watchfulness" here is consistent and needs no register warning. 2. Against its own sibling caption, it does not. §168 gives dran pa the descriptive rendering "Bringing the mind back to the object" rather than the abstract "Mindfulness", while §169 takes the bare abstract noun. The pair is rendered in two different registers on the same chart. §173 then abbreviates both as dran shes and unpacks them in yet a third shape ("effort needed to bring your mind back to the object, and the degree of watchfulness"). Any concordance display of dran pa / shes bzhin across C03 should expect three surface renderings of the same pair; do not auto-resolve them. 3. A wylie/source oddity in the verse at §156: the hook there is shes rab lcags kyu, "the iron hook of your wisdom" — shes rab, not shes bzhin. The chart caption assigns shes bzhin to that panel even though the verse it illustrates says shes rab. Flag for human review rather than harmonizing; the caption text stays verbatim.

AI NOTE — Caption 4 of the elephant-path chart (the caption block runs 167-176) and the longest of them: two Tibetan clauses rendered as three English sentences. The folio marker "4a/" gets no span — editorial apparatus — and neither does its English counterpart "[4]". Every other character of the wylie is covered; the cursor ends on the final yin. MATCHES THE PROSE, WITH ONE IMPORT. This caption restates segment 158, where the six powers are worked out in full: 158's "bla ma'i gdams ngag thos pa'i stobs kyis sems gnas dang po 'grub" is rendered "The first of the states is attained through the power of learning the instructions for meditation from your Lama." Caption 4's Tibetan drops gdams ngag and the Lama, but GMR's English keeps "the instructions" — carried over from the prose, licensed by nothing in this segment. That is why "the instructions" is left unwrapped: thos pa is bare "hearing/learning", and wrapping the object into its span would import 158's vocabulary into 170's evidence. Caption 174 does the same thing ("bsam pa'i stobs so" -> "The power of contemplating the instructions"). The nine states are named at 157; "sems gnas dang po" here is state 1, sems 'jog pa. The one term new to the caption block is khug pa, "bends" — the six bends of the road are a feature of the chart image, not of the prose at 155-160, which never mentions a road. sbyar ba -> "represent". Literally "joining/matching": "as for matching the six bends of the road with the six powers". GMR renders the same verb "is being compared to" at 156 (sbyar te), and uses "represents"/"symbolizes" for a different verb, mtshon, in the neighbouring captions 171-173. "represent" in this block is therefore not a back-key to one Tibetan verb; do not reverse-index it. FOUR NULLS FOR AMBIGUITY, NOT LAZINESS. The Tibetan repeats drug, stobs and dang po; the English repeats "six" and "first" and has "power" only as a substring of "powers". Each first occurrence is linked, each repeat is left null, because a bare repeated token cannot be pointed at and every unique alternative over-captures ("six powers" pulls in the noun, "the power" the article, "first mental" the adjective belonging to sems). Measured first-match positions confirm the kept links land correctly: "six" at 8 ("The six bends"), "first" at 60 ("The first represents"), "represent" at 30 (the standalone form, ahead of "represents"). Also unwrapped and correctly so: "[4]", every article, "in", "represents", and "one" (impersonal — the Tibetan clause ends in yin with no pronoun). DEPTH. One d=7 only: the genitive 'i bound inside thos pa'i, unspaced and immediately following its parent, so the cursor stays strictly monotonic (3, 7, 11, 19, 24, 30, 35, 40, 49, 53, 61, 68, 71, 77, 83, 87, 90, 96, 100, 105, 110, 118, 127). Everything that might have tempted a nested d=7 is flat instead: nas is a space-separated converb syllable after brten (rule 3 names nas as a d=6 case), and sems gnas is given as its two members rather than as a compound parent with children, so no span rewinds inside another. sems gnas is nonetheless a lexical unit — "mental state", one of the nine of 157 — and the sems/gnas pair should display as a compound. khug pa, sbyar ba, thos pa and 'grub pa keep their pa/ba inside the d=5 word: lexicalized, adding no English, and listing them flat would drop bare "pa"/"ba" syllables into a wylie that has four of them.

AI NOTE — Caption 5 of the elephant-path chart. 5a/ is a folio marker fused to the head syllable of glang po, and [5] is the editor's caption number; neither is text, so neither is linked, and the first span begins at glang, not at the start of the string.One Tibetan verb, two English verbs. The wylie is a single clause on the pattern A B dang, C D mtshon — one final verb governing both pairs (elephant→mind, black color→dullness). The English needs a verb in each half, so Geshe Michael renders that one mtshon twice: represents in the first clause, symbolizes in the second. Only one can own the link, and it goes to symbolizes, the finite verb standing where mtshon actually stands. represents is the distributed second realization of the same verb and stays unwrapped — correct and expected, not an omission. The neighbouring caption confirms the pattern rather than the word choice: segment 172 has the identical frame (sprel 'phro ba dang , kha dog nag pa rgod pa mtshon) and renders it "The monkey stands for distraction, and his black color represents agitation." The English verbs are free variants supplied per clause; mtshon is the only one on the page.Two crossings, handled the same way. Tibetan kha dog nag pa is head-then-modifier ("color, black"), English is modifier-then-head ("black color"); Tibetan puts the object before the verb (bying ba mtshon) where English puts it after ("symbolizes dullness"). Both invert. Each is quarantined under a d=5 parent that spans the whole phrase against the whole English phrase — exactly licensed, nothing extra — with the members riding at d=7 inside it. The d=5 layer therefore runs forward in both languages, and the inversion never reaches the top row. This is why mtshon and bying ba are not two flat d=5 spans: listed flat they would cross the cursor.Not linked, deliberately. your in "your mind" and his in "his black color" have no Tibetan licensor — there is no genitive or possessive anywhere in the wylie, only bare sems and kha dog; these are the English supplying the second-person address the chart implies. So sems takes "mind", not "your mind", and the noun phrase takes "black color", not "his black color". The is an article belonging to nobody. The comma and shad are punctuation. po is carried as a null d=7 member of glang po. The nominalizer ba inside bying ba is real but is not listed: bying ba is itself a d=7 member here, and there is no depth below 7 to hang it from — "dullness" already carries it in the -ness counted on its parent.Cross-references. glang po for the mind is not new here: it comes from the Bhavaviveka verse quoted at segment 156, "Master the elephant of the mind" (yid kyi glang po), which the chart illustrates. The caption's bying ba / rgod pa pair, however, is not drawn from the nine-state list — segments 157–159 name the nine mental states, the six powers and the four modes of focus, and dullness and agitation appear in none of them. Their prose treatment comes later: 204 (both abundant in states one and two), 207 (subtle dullness in state five), 208–209, and 190. The rendering of bying ba as "dullness" is stable across all of them, and the black itself is resolved at 191, where glang po'i nag cha zad — "the elephant has lost all the black."
C03/c3p58: AI NOTE — Caption 6 of the elephant-path chart (the nine states of shamatha). Structure: two clauses sharing one clause-final verb — "sprel 'phro ba dang , kha dog nag pa rgod pa mtshon" = "[the] monkey — distraction, and [its] black color — agitation, [these it] represents." Geshe Michael renders the one Tibetan verb as two finite English verbs, "stands for" and "represents". Only one can be licensed by mtshon, so mtshon is linked to "represents", which sits in mtshon's own clause and in the same final position. "stands for" is deliberately left UNWRAPPED — the first clause has no overt Tibetan verb of its own, and double-linking one Tibetan word to two English verbs would manufacture evidence. DIRECT PARALLEL, segment 171: "5a/glang po sems dang , kha dog nag pa bying ba mtshon" = "[5] The elephant represents your mind, and his black color symbolizes dullness." Identical frame, identical kha dog nag pa, identical single final mtshon — but the English distributes the two verbs the other way round (171 puts "represents" in the FIRST clause and "symbolizes" in the second; 172 puts "stands for" first and "represents" second). Anyone aligning 171 should therefore expect mtshon to bind to a different slot than it does here; the two captions are not parallel in their English even though they are parallel in Tibetan. 171/172 are a matched pair: elephant + black = mind + dullness; monkey + black = distraction + agitation. CAPTION VS PROSE. The prose treatment earlier in the course does NOT prepare this vocabulary. Segments 157-159 name the nine mental states and the six powers and four modes of focus, but rgod pa and bying ba appear nowhere in 155-162. The agitation/dullness pair enters the course only with this caption series (171, 172, then 177, 180, 184, 191) and only later returns to prose at 204-212. So the caption is introducing terms, not echoing them. TERM NOTES. rgod pa = "agitation" is stable across the course (177 rgod pa'i yul "the various objects that agitation focuses upon"; 184; 208; 191). "distraction", however, is shared by two different Tibetan words: 'phro ba here and at 185 (sems ... la 'phro ba, rendered verbally as "distracted"), against g-yeng ba at 163 ("give up all distraction") and 181 ("your mind is wandering"). A reverse lookup on "distraction" will pull both; they are not interchangeable — 'phro ba is the mind spilling outward onto another object, g-yeng ba the mind straying. WYLIE ODDITY. The monkey is spelled sprel here; at 191 the same animal in the same chart is spre'u ("left behind the monkey as well"). Both are attested for "monkey" but a string search on either spelling alone will miss half the chart. BOUNDARY DECISIONS. kha dog nag pa is kept as ONE d=5 span rather than split into kha dog = "color" and nag pa = "black": the members would cross, since English puts "black" before "color", which would place a child out of order inside its own phrase. The compound maps onto "black color" exactly, with nothing left over. Unwrapped English, all correct: "[6]" (caption number, matching the folio marker's apparatus status), "The", "stands", "for" (part of the unlinked English phrasal verb, not any Tibetan particle), "and" (see s5), and "his" — there is no genitive or possessive anywhere in the wylie, kha dog nag pa is bare, so "his" has no Tibetan licensor and must not be absorbed into the "black color" span. The shad and comma between dang and kha dog are punctuation and are not linked.

AI NOTE — Caption [7] of the numbered legend to the elephant-path (shamatha) chart described at §156-§166. Not linked as apparatus: the wylie's "7a/" and the English's "[7]". Wylie oddity worth recording: these markers are not folio sides — §176 has "1a0/" for [10] and §178 "1a2/" for [12], so the "a" is a slot filler sitting between digits. The marker simply restates the caption number. THE SUBSTANTIVE CORRECTION TO BOTH PROPOSALS. A and B independently agreed that "to bring your mind back to the object" is an unlicensed expansion — B called it "Geshe Michael's gloss of what the effort is for." It is not. In this very caption series, §168 renders the bare wylie "dran pa" as "Bringing the mind back to the object", §169 renders "shes bzhin" as "Watchfulness", and §158 gives "dran pa'i stobs" as "the power of bringing your mind back to the object" against "shes bzhin gyi stobs" as "the power of watchfulness". dran shes here is the standing abbreviation of that pair, and the English distributes it: "...effort needed to bring your mind back to the object, and the degree of watchfulness needed." So dran and shes each have a real exponent and are linked at d=7 (s25, s26), and the parent dran shes is null — a contiguous English span covering both members would have to swallow ", and the degree of", which is exactly the over-capture the audits flag. Both proposals' dran shes = "watchfulness" gave the whole compound only its second member's English. Term check against the prose, since the caption is meant to gloss it. sems gnas bdun pa matches §157-§158 word for word (same sems gnas + ordinal frame; §158 uses bdun pa for the seventh). But the caption's word for effort is 'bad rtsol, whereas §158 assigns the seventh and eighth states to brtson 'grus kyi stobs, "the power of effort". These are different Tibetan words sharing one English word, and they are not making the same claim: §158's brtson 'grus is the power that produces states 7-8, while the caption's 'bad rtsol is the exertion of mindfulness-and-watchfulness whose magnitude the flames depict from state 1 up to state 7. A translator should not merge them, and a concordance on "effort" will pull both. Note also that §158 assigns dran pa to states 3-4 and shes bzhin to 5-6, while the caption runs their joint effort across the whole span up to 7. Boundary rulings taken from the two proposals. (1) 'di nas is split (A) rather than kept whole as "from this point" (B): "point" has no Tibetan licensor and stays unwrapped; nas = "from" is a single occurrence and is the ablative's proper exponent. (2) che chung gi khyad par is split (A) rather than kept whole as "relative size" / "relative amount" (B): "size" and "amount" are each single occurrences and are exactly what che chung licenses, while "relative" occurs twice and is therefore unlinkable, so khyad par is null in both places. Splitting does not force "relative" onto khyad par — nothing goes onto khyad par. This also settles the two proposals' gi depth disagreement: with che chung and khyad par listed separately, gi is a space-separated syllable between two listed d=5 spans, so it is d=6, not B's d=7. The kyi at s27 is d=6 for the same reason. Every genuinely bound morpheme is d=7: the two pa's, and the members of sems gnas, me lce, yod med, che chung (both occurrences) and dran shes. A's ro at d=5 "copula" is demoted to d=6 and nulled — it is a particle, and per the reconciliation rule the doubtful link goes unwrapped. Compounds are decomposed at d=7 only where the members carry distinct sense the fused English hides (sems gnas, me lce, yod med, che chung, dran shes). 'bad rtsol and stobs shugs are left whole: they are synonym-doublets ('bad pa / rtsol ba both "exertion"; stobs / shugs both "force"), and splitting them would yield nulls recording nothing. Crossing: the English opens with the flames clause (me lce yod med dang che chung gi khyad par, mid-sentence in the Tibetan) and only then gives 'di nas...bar, which opens the Tibetan. Span order below follows the Tibetan; the English positions therefore run backwards at the start. Deliberately unwrapped English, no Tibetan licensor: both instances of "relative"; "point"; "the degree"; every article; both instances of "needed"; "represent" (see s36); and "of the flames" and "their", where the possessive relation is juxtaposition rather than a particle. Mechanically verified against the spine row: all 36 tib values are contiguous substrings resolved by a strict forward-only cursor (che chung / gi / khyad par each occur twice and are listed first-then-second); every d=7 span is a substring of the d=5 span it hangs under; every non-null eng value occurs exactly once in the English; and the d=5/d=6 layer covers all 34 wylie tokens after the marker, in order, with nothing doubled and nothing missing.

AI NOTE — Caption 8 of the nine-stage elephant-path chart (dbu ma snying po's taming-the-elephant simile, introduced at §156). It names the second of the six powers and the mental state that power accomplishes. CROSS-REFERENCE — the caption against the prose. §158 treats the same stage in running prose: "bsam pa'i stobs kyis gnyis pa 'grub" / "The second is reached through the power of contemplating these instructions." The caption's Tibetan is the same clause with two changes: it spells out sems gnas where the prose has a bare ordinal gnyis pa, and it carries the power in a resumptive 'dis instead of stobs kyis. HGM's English tracks that: "the power of contemplating" is word-for-word identical in both places, and the caption's "the instructions" answers the prose's "these instructions" — which is the direct evidence that "instructions" here is supplied from §158, not translated from this segment. The second state itself is rgyun du 'jog pa per the §157 list, captioned separately at §175 as "2) Keeping the mind on the object with brief continuity"; §174 does not name it, it only numbers it. So: wording matches the prose treatment, with the caption compressed and the object of contemplation carried over. A TERM TAKING A NEW RENDERING. The resumptive demonstrative-plus-instrumental is rendered three different ways across the three power captions: §170 'di la brten nas → "Based on this"; §174 'dis → "You use this to"; §178 'dis → "This allows you to". Same Tibetan, three English periphrases, none of them a preposition. That is exactly why the -s is nulled rather than linked — there is no stable English exponent to point at, and each rendering distributes the case force across a different verb. WYLIE ODDITY. §174's stobs is spelled correctly; the parallel caption §178 reads "dran pa'i ltobs so", an l- for s- typo in the source keying. Flag it there, not here. Also worth knowing for the apparatus: the chart's markers run 1a/ ... 9a/ then 1a0/, 1a1/ ... 1a6/, i.e. the caption number with an 'a' infix, matching [1]–[16] in the English one for one. So "8a/" is the caption-number marker, not a folio reference — both proposals called it a folio marker, and both were wrong about that; it stays unlinked either way. RECONCILIATION. - Depth/segmentation: took B's head-plus-bound-morpheme form (bsam pa + 'i, 'di + s) over A's parent-then-children form (bsam pa'i then pa then 'i; 'dis then s; sems gnas then sems then gnas; gnyis pa then pa). A's depths were right in principle — those morphemes are bound and are d=7 — but listing a parent and then its own pieces tiles ground the forward cursor has already passed. Concretely: after "bsam pa'i" the cursor sits at 12 and the next "pa" is at 44, inside gnyis pa; after "'dis" the cursor sits at 27 and the next "s" is at 28, inside sems. Both would silently link the wrong syllables. A's sems/gnas and its ordinal pa are absent forward of their parents and would be refused outright. The bound morphemes keep d=7; they are just listed as the tail of the word rather than as a re-cut of it. - so is d=6, correctly, in both proposals: it is a standalone syllable with spaces on both sides, not a piece of stobs. - Boundaries: tighter English taken throughout. 'grub owns "reach" only, not "to reach". gnyis pa owns "second"; sems gnas owns "mental state" with no numeral folded in. - Left unwrapped, with no Tibetan licensor: "[8]", both "The"/"the" articles (and "the" occurs twice regardless, so rule 5 bars it independently), "the instructions" (no gdams ngag or man ngag anywhere in this segment — compare §158, which does have bla ma'i gdams ngag for the first power), "You use", and the infinitival "to". - Checked for rule 5: "of", "this", "second", "power", "reach", "mental" each occur exactly once in the English, so every link is unambiguous.
C03/c3p59: AI NOTE — Four spans on a three-word caption: the name of the second of the nine mental states (sems gnas dgu), captioning the elephant-path chart. CROSS-REFERENCE TO THE PROSE LIST AT C03:157 — verified exact. AI NOTE — Reconciled from a Tibetan-first (A) and an English-first (B) walk. Verified against the spine: wylie `rgya mtsho dang ni ri rab dang , ,sa rnams bdag gi khur min gyi, ,byas pa mi gzo gang yin pa, ,de ni bdag gi khur chen yin, ,zhes dang`. STRUCTURE. A quoted verse closed by the citation formula `zhes dang`. Three subjects in a dang-list (rgya mtsho / ri rab / sa rnams) share one predicate `bdag gi khur min`; the adversative `gyi` pivots to the counter-claim `byas pa mi gzo gang yin pa de ni bdag gi khur chen yin` — literally "whatever fails to repay kindness done, THAT is my great burden." ENGLISH ORDER IS NOT MONOTONIC, correctly. GMR fronts "My calling's rather to attend" (wylie position 4) ahead of "never fail Repaying kindness granted me" (wylie position 3). Spans are in wylie order per rule 2; their English jumps backwards and forwards, which is expected here and is not a cursor error. WHAT A TRANSLATOR NEEDS — the khur problem. `khur` (burden/load) occurs twice in the wylie and is rendered FOUR ways in the English: "problem", "task", "job", and — for `khur chen` — "calling". This is a live register split, evidenced at span level inside this one segment, and it is the single fact to carry forward: GMR varies the English lexeme for rhythm across parallel clauses while the Tibetan repeats one word. Do not let a concordance conclude that khur means "job". (None of the three registered register splits — gus pa, skyabs su 'gro, mchog 'dzin — occur in this segment.) DISTRIBUTED PREDICATE, deliberately under-covered. `bdag gi khur min` is predicated once but surfaces three times: "is not my problem", "My task is not", "My job is not". One Tibetan phrase against three English exponents — unequal counts, which do not resolve (rule 6). Keyed to the first and nearest exponent only; "My task is not" and "My job is not" are left UNWRAPPED rather than double-keying or fabricating a discontiguous span (rule 7). The subject nouns still carry their own spans, so "the mountains" and "the earth" remain attributed even though their predicates are not. DISAGREEMENTS RESOLVED - `bdag gi khur min` — took B's constituent predicate over A's four separate spans (A nulled bdag gi and min on a GLOBAL ambiguity count; rule 4 measures uniqueness INSIDE THE PARENT, and "my", "problem", "not" are each unique within "is not my problem"). B's member was `bdag` → "my"; widened by one syllable to `bdag gi`, because the genitive is what supplies the possessive. Still tight, still unique in the parent. - `mi gzo` — took A's TIGHTER "fail Repaying" over B's "never fail Repaying", and A's mi → "fail" over B's mi → "never". "fail Repaying" IS `mi gzo` exactly; "never" belongs to GMR's polarity inversion of the whole clause ("my calling is that I should never fail...") and has no Tibetan exponent, so it stays outside the span. This is the boundary-disagreement rule and the semantics agreeing. - `gyi` → null, taking B. A keyed it to "rather", which is verbatim English but sits four clauses downstream in a different sentence; the conservative reading holds. - `byas pa` → "kindness granted", taking B's tighter boundary. A included "me", which `byas pa` does not license (the beneficiary is implied, not stated). - `bdag gi khur chen yin` → "My calling's", taking B on rule 8. A split "My calling" out of "My calling's", breaking a word at the apostrophe; the "'s" is the copula `yin`, but a non-negative affix may not be broken, so `yin` gets no member and the parent carries the whole phrase. - d=7 spans with null English (B's `rgya`, `rab`) dropped per rule 3. `rnams` and the nominaliser in `byas pa` likewise have no exponent and are omitted. - Final `dang` kept (A had it, B dropped it); it is in the wylie and completes `zhes dang`. NOT ERRATA, checked and dismissed - `ri rab` is Mount Meru, rendered "the mountains". Translational generalisation in a verse register, not an error; the d=7 member ri → "mountains" is sound (ri rab = supreme mountain), `rab` has no exponent. - ACIP "MTSO" for `mtsho` is correct ACIP orthography (tsh → TS, ts → TZ). Verified in the spine: 1219 segments contain MTSO, 0 contain MTSHO. - The " , ," shad spacing is normal ACIP-derived punctuation. - Tibetan spelling audit clean throughout: rgya mtsho, ri rab, sa rnams, khur min gyi (correct connective after final -na), byas pa mi gzo (cf. gzo ba, "requite"), gang yin pa, khur chen yin. MECHANICAL CHECK before submission: every tib is a contiguous substring of the wylie under a forward-only cursor; every eng is a contiguous substring of the English; every d=7 tib is a substring of its parent's tib and every d=7 eng a substring of its parent's eng, each unique within that parent. "not" (3 global occurrences) and "My" (3) are globally ambiguous but unique inside their parents, which is where rule 4 measures.

UNWRAPPED BY DESIGN (rule 7). Three pieces of English are deliberately not keyed to Tibetan: - "say the lines," -- GMR's supplied attribution formula. The wylie has only 'gzhan yang' introducing the citation: no verb of speaking, no noun for "lines". Its Tibetan counterpart is 'zhes pa ltar', which opens C03:320, not this segment. Folding it into s01 would be over-capture. - the article "A" in "A kindness returned" -- no Tibetan exponent. - the footnote digits "13" -- see errata. STRUCTURE: THE PHRASE NODES ARE LOAD-BEARING, NOT COSMETIC. 'drin la lan' and 'drin gzo med pa' are spanned as d=5 phrases with d=7 members rather than as flat top-level words. In the English, "kindness" occurs twice and "returned" occurs twice (once free, once inside "unreturned"); flat top-level spans would leave both as unequal-count ambiguities under rule 6 and the page would refuse. Nested, each member is unique inside its parent -- verified: "kindness" and "returned" each occur exactly once in "kindness returned" and exactly once in "kindness unreturned" -- so rule 4 is satisfied and the ambiguity never arises. The same nesting is what makes 'drin' resolvable on the Tibetan side: it occurs twice in the full wylie but exactly once inside each parent. 'gzhan' IS NULLED, NOT DROPPED (s02). It has no exponent in "So too", but it is a pronoun, not a bound particle, so rule 3's leave-it-out clause does not reach it; rule 5 governs and it takes eng: null. The reader should see that the idiom has two members and that only one surfaces in English. NEGATIVE-AFFIX CONVENTION (s12, s13). 'med' owns the "un" of "unreturned" and 'gzo' ("to repay") owns the stem "returned"; both are marked subword, the only breaking of an English word rule 8 permits. 'med' is preferred over 'med pa' as the tighter span -- the negation lives in 'med', and 'pa' is a nominaliser with no exponent, so 'pa' is left out under rule 3. Member order follows the wylie (drin, gzo, med) while the English order inverts; rule 2 permits this, since only the Tibetan cursor is forward-only. PARTICLES DROPPED. 'la' (dative on drin) and 'pa' (nominaliser on med) are bound particles with no English and are left out per rule 3. 'ste' is standalone and does surface, so it is kept at d=6 owning "And" -- it is the semi-final connective joining the two verse lines, and "And" is exactly that coordination surfacing at the head of line two. Sole occurrence of "And", no ambiguity. "is" RESOLVES BY EQUAL COUNT. "is" occurs exactly twice in the English and exactly two spans claim it: 'yod' (existential, first clause -- the only verb in 'drin la lan yod bzang po ste', so the "is" of "is goodness" rests on it) and 'yin' (copula, second clause). Equal counts, so it resolves in order under rule 6. 'bzang po' IS NOT SPLIT. "good" inside "goodness" would be a broken word outside the negative-affix exception (rule 8), so 'bzang po' takes the whole of "goodness". Same for 'ngan pa' / "evil". No agentive -s occurs in this segment, so rule 9 does not bite. FOR THE TRANSLATOR. The line is a proverb built on a chiasmus: drin la lan yod / bzang po :: drin gzo med pa / ngan pa. 'lan' (a return) and 'gzo' (to repay) are the noun and verb sides of one idea, which is why both surface as "returned" in the English; they should not be read as two different concepts. 'drin gzo' is well attested across the spine -- 28 segments contain it by wylie substring match (C01:280, 299, 301; C03:317, 319, 320, 322; C04:111; C07:34, 53, 55; C11:480; C16 x6; C17:112, 114; TCS02 x2; TCS03:52; TCS14:107; P1:12, 13, 15; TITLS:614) -- and the immediate context sets it up: C03:317 "give no thought to returning it", C03:318 "Repaying kindness granted me", C03:320 'drin gzo ba dgos' / "now that we must repay them". Treat 28 as a lower bound on real attestations: it counts only the exact string 'drin gzo' and misses 'drin lan' phrasings such as C03:320's 'drin lan bsab pa'. REGISTER. None of the three recorded register splits (gus pa, skyabs su 'gro, mchog 'dzin) occurs in this segment, so no register warning attaches here. Worth flagging separately for a human: 'bzang po' / 'ngan pa' are rendered here as the nominals "goodness" / "evil" in a verse register, where the same pair reads "good" / "bad" in prose (compare C03:317's "an evil way to act" for 'lugs ngan pa'). That is a verse-vs-prose register difference in GMR's own English, not a defect, and not auto-resolvable. ORTHOGRAPHY. The wylie is sound throughout; no spelling defect found. The ' , , ' and ', ,' sequences are ordinary verse-line shad punctuation, not ingest damage -- P1:12 carries the same line with lighter shad spacing and identical syllables. RECONCILIATION RECORD. Proposal A and Proposal B agreed on the title, on the errata, on 'ste' -> "And" at d=6, on the negative-affix treatment of "unreturned", and on leaving "say the lines," unwrapped. Three disagreements were decided: (1) structure -- B's nested phrase nodes taken over A's flat 'drin' / 'la' / 'lan', because A's layout leaves "kindness" claimed once against two occurrences, an unequal-count failure under rule 6; (2) 'gzhan' -- B's explicit null taken over A's omission, since rule 5 covers a word with no exponent and rule 3's leave-it-out clause covers only bound particles; (3) 'med pa' vs 'med' -- B's 'med' taken as the tighter span on a boundary disagreement. A's richer cls glosses were carried into B's skeleton. B's claim of 64 trailing-digit segments in C03 was re-run and confirmed; A's claim that P1:12 is a word-for-word parallel without the digits was re-run and confirmed, and it is the strongest single piece of errata evidence, so it leads the entry.

SHARED FORMULAE this folio runs on two recurring frames, both now attested three times ├─ DEFINITION [definiens] X-gi mtshan nyid → "The definition of X is '…'" (inverted every time) └─ DIVISION de la sgras brjod rigs kyi sgo nas dbye na → "In name only, this Jewel can be divided" ├─ sgras brjod rigs "the class of verbal expression" "In name only" — GMR's compression of the scholastic tag ├─ sgo nas "through the door of" ∅ · na conditional "can be" └─ 'gog lam gang rung gis bsdus pa'i "subsumed by cessation or path, whichever" "either in the form of a cessation, or in the form of a path, or both"
C02/p05: THE REFUGE FORMULA this skeleton returns, expanded, five times in segs 39–45 — learn it once here ├─ OBLIQUE · la-frame yul gzhan la "toward another object" "that some object outside of one's self" │ └─ la marks the target of the hope; GMR moves it inside the "hoping that" clause ├─ MANNER · agentive frame rang stobs kyis "by its own power" "that acts of its own accord" ├─ CORE · the hope dpung gnyen du re ba 'cha' ba'i │ ├─ dpung gnyen n. "reinforcement, ally" "render one assistance" ("will be able to" is his modality) │ ├─ du la-group: "as (an ally)" ∅ — absorbed into the verb phrase │ └─ re ba 'cha' ba'i "forming a hope" + ba'i "consists of hoping" └─ HEAD sems pa the mental factor cetanā "movement of the mind" — see note
